title: NebulaForge capacity readiness, burst & isolation review
summary: Discovery with NebulaForge to map expected peak QPS, isolation requirements for PII workloads, and a two-phase pilot: hosted fallback + Dedicated reserved pool. Key ask: how to handle bursts without blowing committed spend and how to guarantee isolation for regulated customers.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-04-21
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Recording: enabled
- Attendees: Alice Park (Redwood AE); Ben Ortiz (Redwood SE); Maya Singh (Redwood SE); Clara Ruiz (NebulaForge CTO); Jake Morrison (Infra Lead); Priya Patel (ML Platform); Samir Khanna (Procurement)

Summary (auto):
NebulaForge runs a multi-tenant inference platform serving customer-facing agents and internal analytics. They are evaluating Redwood Dedicated for a mix of latency-sensitive agents and batch scoring. Main constraints: need for dedicated isolation for a subset of customers (regulatory), desire to avoid over-committing GPUs for rare bursts, and procurement timeline of ~6-8 weeks. They want a pilot that proves tail latency under 99th percentile SLOs and a cost model that blends reserved capacity with burst credits or overflow to Redwood Hosted.

Topics covered: reserved sizing approach, isolation options (single-tenant nodes vs VPC+network policies), burst strategies (pre-warmed pools, overflow to hosted, autoscale), monitoring/telemetry requirements, security concerns (SOC2, KMS, SAML), contract/pricing model and procurement timing.

Action items (recap in call, not formal): send sizing spreadsheet; schedule benchmark run; share security/arch docs; draft pilot statement of work.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alice (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll keep to 45 minutes but leave some time for Qs. Quick intros?
[00:08] Clara (NebulaForge CTO): Hi all, Clara here. We're building the conversational agents for ecommerce ops, also running internal scoring jobs. Looking to understand how Redwood can fit both low-latency and batch workflows.
[00:16] Ben (SE): Great, Clara. Ben from Redwood. I'll focus on architecture and how we size dedicated pools. Quick question up front — do you have a target 99th percentile latency for those agents?
[00:26] Priya (ML Platform): For customer-facing agents we want under 250ms p99 for 2k concurrent connections; internal scoring can be looser, like 500–700ms. Those are ballpark.
[00:37] Jake (Infra): Also an important note — a subset of our customers are regulated and must be isolated. We need options that give physical or tenant isolation, or at least guaranteed compute lines.
[00:47] Ben (SE): Understood. Redwood Dedicated supports node-level isolation and private deployments. We can do dedicated GPU pools where nodes are reserved for your org only, plus VPC peering for network-level separation. There are tradeoffs — single-tenant nodes cost more but remove noisy neighbor risk.
[00:59] Clara: Can you describe the burst model? We see large diurnal bursts; peaks are maybe 10x baseline for 15–30 minutes a few times per day. We don't want to pay for 10x all the time.
[01:12] Ben: Typical patterns we recommend: a committed reserved pool sized to cover baseline + steady spikes, and burst handled with a combination of two mechanisms: (1) pre-warmed buffer nodes that are inexpensive to keep ready, and (2) overflow to Redwood Hosted endpoints that throttle-cost but maintain availability. You can also combine with autoscaling and short-lived preemptible instances if acceptable.
[01:31] Priya: Overflow to Hosted — are there data residency or encryption concerns? Some of this traffic contains PII.
[01:37] Maya (SE): Good call. Hosted endpoints can be used for non-PII or anonymized request paths; for regulated customers we advise using Dedicated or Private with KMS integration. We have KMS/HSM options and can integrate with your key provider. For data residency, Private deployment into your VPC or on-prem is the path.
[01:56] Jake: What's involved in Private deployment? We have air-gapped customers, so we might need no outbound connectivity.
[02:02] Ben: Private involves a customer-managed control plane option, can support air-gapped installs with an on-prem package. That increases lead time and procurement complexity. For majority of cases, VPC + dedicated nodes is enough.
[02:16] Clara: Back to cost — can Redwood provide a blended price if we commit to monthly GPUs but occasionally use hosted overflow?
[02:23] Alice (AE): Yes, we typically structure a reserved commit with a capped monthly fee and a separate burst/overflow pricing tier. We can do committed usage credits that you draw down when overflow occurs; we can propose tiered rates for overflow to reduce cost shock. We'll include examples in the pricing spreadsheet.
[02:39] Samir (Procurement): Procurement timeline — we usually need SOW, SOC2 docs, and an MSA with indemnities. How long does Redwood take for standard enterprise legal?
[02:47] Alice: For mid-market contracts we average 4–8 weeks; enterprise with security reviews can be 8–12. We have standard SOC2 reports and can provide security architecture docs. Ben and Maya will share those materials.
[02:57] Priya: On the ops side, how do we handle KV cache warmup and long context windows? Our agents pass around session history up to 8k tokens.
[03:07] Ben: Redwood runtime manages KV cache and supports optimized kernels for long context. For 8k contexts we recommend quantization profiles and sufficient GPU memory in the dedicated nodes. We'll recommend exact GPU class once we see your sequence length distribution — Ben to collect histograms.
[03:22] Jake: We also need to ensure that failover from Dedicated to Hosted doesn't leak logs or keys. What's the pattern?
[03:29] Maya: Failover we recommend is at the request routing layer: sensitive customers flagged as "no-fallback" and remain on Dedicated, non-sensitive flagged to be permitted to overflow. Our routing can annotate requests; logs only flow to customer S3/KMS if configured. We'll send details on how logs and telemetry are partitioned.
[03:47] Clara: Do you support pinning models/versions per customer? We need reproducibility for audits.
[03:53] Ben: Yes — model pinning and rollout policies are first-class. You can pin a specific version and we support canary deploys and automatic fallback to pinned versions if new model fails.
[04:04] Priya: For the pilot, we're thinking 4–6 weeks: first week baseline integration and runbook, 2–3 weeks benching and shadow traffic, final week soak and SLA measurement. Is that realistic?
[04:14] Alice: That matches our typical pilot. We recommend an initial reserved pool sized for baseline and a burst plan so we can exercise overflow paths.
[04:21] Jake: On monitoring — we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency histograms.
[04:26] Maya: Console provides token-level cost, per-route latency, traces, and error analysis. We can export to your Datadog/Splunk. Exports are configurable.
[04:35] Ben: A couple more technical notes — if you choose preemptible burst nodes, we recommend mixing with persistent reserved nodes to prevent tail latency spikes. Also continuous batching parameters are tunable per model.
[04:46] Priya: Any competitive considerations? We compare self-hosted runtimes and a large cloud vendor. What do you see as main trade-offs?
[04:53] Ben: Self-hosting gives control but higher ops cost; large cloud endpoints give scale but limited kernel optimizations and less predictable p99 in many cases. Redwood aims to be predictable for production with observability and cost controls.
[05:07] Clara: Ok, let's close with next steps.
[05:09] Alice: Recap of next steps — Ben will send sizing spreadsheet for you to fill in (sequence length histogram, qps by hour, percent of PII traffic), Maya will share security/SOC2/KMS docs, Alice will draft a pilot SOW and example pricing with reserved + overflow options, and we'll schedule a benchmark run in two weeks.
[05:27] Samir: Procurement will want sample MSA and redlines; we'll attach to the SOW.
[05:31] Clara: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[05:33] Alice: Thank you — we'll follow up with all artifacts.

End transcript.
